The Türk Khaganates were steppe empires ruled by the Ashina clan of the Göktürks, from 552 to 744, first from Mongolia across Inner Asia. They were the first state to use the name Türk, and the first to stretch from Manchuria to the Black Sea.

In 552 Bumin Qaghan overthrew his overlords, the Rouran Khaganate. His brother Istämi led the western wing. Within twenty years the Türks ruled the whole steppe and, with Sasanian Iran, destroyed the Hephthalites around 560.

The Türks controlled much of the Silk Road. Sogdian merchants worked for them, and their first official texts and coins were in Sogdian. They sent envoys as far as the Eastern Roman Empire, hoping to sell silk without Persian middlemen.

Their history ran in two phases:

  • First Khaganate, 552 to 603: split by civil war into eastern and western halves.
  • Tang China conquered the eastern Türks in 630 and the western Türks by 657.
  • Second Khaganate, 682 to 744: the eastern Türks broke free again. Its leaders raised the Orkhon inscriptions in the 730s, the earliest long texts in a Turkic language.
  • 744: overthrown by the Uyghur Khaganate.

Their real legacy is the name and the language. The Turkic migrations that followed carried Turkic speech from Mongolia to Anatolia.
